results.title: Nebius Raises AI GPU Cloud Prices as Compute Demand Surges
highlights:
Nebius is raising pay-as-you-go prices for selected NVIDIA GPU cloud instances as demand for artificial intelligence computing continues to strain available capacity.

Beginning October 1, selected NVIDIA GPU rates will increase roughly 17% to 21%, according to Reuters. Some CPU-only instances will rise about 25%, while selected memory offerings will increase about 41%. The move marks Nebius’ second price increase in three months.

The increases provide another signal that the AI infrastructure boom is extending beyond GPUs. Large AI clusters also require substantial power, cooling, networking, CPUs and memory, putting pressure across the physical data-center stack.

Nebius said customers reserving large-scale clusters for multiple months can receive commitment discounts. Reuters also reported that the company’s recent AI cloud growth included four customer contracts averaging more than $1 billion each.

results.title: The Blackwell shortage playbook: finding B200/B300 capacity without paying the hyperscaler premium — CheapestGPU
highlights:
The "B200/B300 shortage" is not one number. It is a packaging constraint stacked on a hyperscaler forward-order queue, and the fix is reading confirmed versus unconfirmed capacity on an order book, not chasing whichever headline discount shows up first.

...

The binding constraint is packaging, not wafers. Troy Technical's August 9, 2026 report on the CoWoS bottleneck states TSMC CEO C.C. Wei confirmed in June 2026 that CoWoS-L advanced-packaging capacity remained "extremely tight and sold out through 2026," even as TSMC targets 125,000 to 130,000 wafers/month by year-end. The same report puts Nvidia's 2026 CoWoS bookings at roughly 800,000 to 850,000 wafers, about 60% of TSMC's total output on Morgan Stanley's estimate, locking in packaging for Blackwell Ultra (B300) and next-generation Rubin silicon at the same time. CoWoS demand is running 40 to 50 percent above supply, and enterprise buyers are seeing Blackwell delivery slip into Q1 2027 because packaging allocation, not wafer supply, is the ceiling.

That packaging squeeze shows up directly in list prices. Shattered's 2026 report on Nebius' pricing states the neocloud raised GPU rental rates by up to 21% effective October 1, 2026 - B300 from $7.85 to $9.50/GPU-hr (about 21%), B200 from $7.15 to $8.50/GPU-hr (about 19%). It is Nebius' second hike in 2026: an earlier May pass raised on-demand rates roughly 29% and spot rates roughly 51%, so the current B300 rate sits about 56% above its pre-May level of roughly $6.10/GPU-hr. Read that as market context on where hyperscaler-adjacent neocloud pricing is heading, not as a CheapestGPU board rate.

...

Thunder Compute's September 2026 B200 pricing pass, tracking 11 providers, put the on-demand floor at $5.99/GPU-hr (Hyperbolic) against a $16.11/GPU-hr ceiling (Google Cloud) - a single B200 running 24/7 for a month costs about $4,313 at the floor versus $11,599 at the ceiling, a spread of roughly 2.7x for the same silicon. That comparison is cited market data, useful for orienting yourself, but it is not a CheapestGPU listing.

The order book carries exactly two live B200 rows today, and both are SXM, 36-month reserved, 20% prepayment - there is no PCIe or on-demand B200 row on the board right now:

- `io-b200-512-2026` (`data/listingsIo.ts`): 512x B200 SXM, $3.84/GPU-hr, NVLink 5 / NVSwitch intra-node, IB-ready NDR400 (CX-7 VPI) inter-node, location "Reserved - RFS TBD", proposal-backed (`IO-B200-512-2026`), $10,333,716.48 prepayment at signing. At the board's 730-hours/month baseline: $3.84 x 730 = $2,803/GPU/month; the full 512-GPU row is $2,803 x 512 = ~$1,435,238/month.
- `cap-b200-256-hot-2026` (`data/listingsBaremetal.ts`): 256x B200 SXM, $3.85/GPU-hr, Full NDR InfiniBand + leaf/spine + OOB management, Tier III datacenter (location TBD), capacity-board row with no attachment, $4,843,929.60 prepayment at signing. At 730 hours/month: $3.85 x 730 = $2,810.50/GPU/month; the full 256-GPU row is $719,488/month.

Both rows carry the same commitment shape (SXM, 36 months, 20% down), so the "spread" claim above cannot be compared sticker-to-sticker against them - it is an hourly on-demand rate against a signed multi-year reserved price. Compare like commitment types, not like GPU models.

...

Using the two real B200 rows above against Thunder Compute's cited on-demand band: $2,803/$4,313 (neocloud floor) is about 65%, and $2,803/$11,599 (hyperscaler ceiling) is about 24%. The `cap-b200-256-hot-2026` row lands at nearly the same ratios ($2,810.50/$4,313 and $2,810.50/$11,599). In plain terms: if you would run this capacity more than about two-thirds of the term hours, either board reserved rate beats even the cheapest tracked neocloud on-demand price; against the hyperscaler ceiling, breakeven drops under a quarter utilization. The catch is the term floor - both rows require signing 36 months with 20% down to get there. Neither can be signed for 30 or 90 days; a shorter job has to go through on-demand or a custom term negotiated over Message.

results.title: Adam Sioud | Modelling GPU rental prices
highlights:
GPU rental prices go up and down. There are small day-to-day changes, longer trends and periods when prices move more sharply. I’m interested in these patterns and what they might tell me about demand picking up or capacity becoming harder to find, and the reasons behind price changes.

For this article, there is a good example to look at in May 2026. RTX 3090 asking prices on Vast.ai rose sharply, then fell back in June. And there was a dataset on Hugging Face with data on these listings. So I wanted to explore it. I don’t know exactly what drove the move, but there is data to work with. How can I wrangle it and play with it to get a clearer picture of what happened?

...

In mid-May, prices begin to leave that range. On May 30, the index reaches 240.1, while the baseline is 105.4: 128% above its baseline.

The main period above the range runs from May 14 to June 13, 31 days, using three consecutive days outside the band to identify a sustained change. Prices then fall back towards the baseline.

...

On May 30, 39 of 40 sellers were more than 10% above their April prices. Raising the threshold to 100% still leaves 34 of 40. For most of these sellers, prices had more than doubled.

The price rise lasted several weeks and involved most of the sellers that were tracked. Prices increased on individual listings, so cheaper offers disappearing cannot explain the rise on its own. Each search returns at most 64 listings, so this describes the sellers in the sample, but should still be indicative of the wider price movement.

...

#### Pearl mining

Miners were renting GPUs to earn Pearl’s PRL token during the price rise. Tom’s Hardware reported on May 31 that miners were using RTX 4090 and 5090 instances on Vast.ai and RunPod, while a June study also reported people earning PRL on rented RTX 3090s. Alongside these reports, network hash rate shows the increase in mining activity, which is a big tell that mining PRL was directly linked to renting listings on Vast.ai.

So in a situation where PRL earnings can cover the rental cost and fees, miners have a reason to rent available listings, creating a strong incentive and big demand for the GPUs listed. As more listings are rented, buyers are left competing for less available capacity. In turn, that gives sellers an incentive to raise their asking prices. I think it’s clear that this demand from Pearl miners very likely contributed to the broad repricing in May. And while this was a sharper surge, we now also see more sustained demand affecting overall prices since the summer. So this is not a one-off event, in my opinion, and needs to be understood and studied more.

In addition, other GPU rental prices were rising too. AIMC’s report for May 25–31 recorded average on-demand prices up 4.9% for H100 SXM and 8.8% for H200 SXM. Very interesting.

results.title: 13 new GPU clouds; cheapest H100 SXM still $1.79, September 2026
highlights:
On 2026-09-26 our table holds 581 rate quotes from 51 clouds across 40 GPU models. Ninety-six of those quotes are one day old: thirteen providers were read for the first time on the evening of 2026-09-25 — Akamai Cloud (Linode), EmpirioLabs, Civo, Daytona, Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, HexGrid, Lyceum, Canopy Wave, Atlas Cloud, Neysa, Nova Cloud, Enverge and EcoHash. Between them they list an on-demand rate card on 29 of the 40 cards. On 26 of those 29, the cheapest rate card belongs to a seller that was already in the table.

## The cheapest H100 SXM is still $1.79

Twenty-five clouds list an on-demand H100 SXM on 2026-09-26. The median rate card — each provider counted once, at its own cheapest on-demand rate, community capacity and marketplace floors left out — is $3.61 per GPU-hour, over a 6.2x spread from $1.79 at Cudo Compute in no-kristiansand-1 to $11.06 at Microsoft Azure in eastus.

Five of the thirteen list the card, and all five landed in the middle of it: Atlas Cloud at $2.95, Civo and HexGrid at $2.99, Canopy Wave at $3.25 (priced per GPU on a two-GPU machine) and Neysa at $4.39, which its page prints as a from rate. The cheapest of the twenty-five, Cudo’s $1.79, has read the same in every one of our hourly reads since 2026-09-07, the day we first read it.

...

## The two near misses

Daytona came second on the B300 at $6.25 for a GPU-only rate, behind Sesterce’s $4.95 from rate, against a median of $7.99 across fifteen providers. Hugging Face came second on the T4 at $0.50 for a single card on AWS, behind Google Cloud’s $0.35 in us-east5, against a median of $0.56 across eight providers.

results.title: AI compute got dearer in September, and data centres are being handed the grid bill | ByteNib
highlights:
CoreWeave is signing short GPU contracts at about $40m a megawatt, Oracle's $664bn backlog came with negative free cash flow, and US regulators moved to make data centres pay for grid upgrades. What that means for capacity plans.

## In brief

The clearest price signal of September came from a specialist GPU cloud, not a hyperscaler. CoreWeave said it is signing three-to-six-month contracts at about $40 million per megawatt of annualised revenue. Short terms at high prices mean the seller sets the price. Oracle showed the other side of the same market: a $664 billion contract backlog, record deliveries of capacity, and free cash flow of about minus $5.4 billion for the quarter.

US regulators, meanwhile, spent the second half of the month making data centres pay for the grid upgrades they need. For anyone planning AI capacity, the result is higher unit prices, shorter terms, more risk concentrated in a few suppliers and customers, and new sites that cost more and take longer.

...

- CoreWeave (16–17 September). The company says that since 30 June it has kept contracting capacity "at higher prices". That includes short-dated contracts at about $40 million per megawatt, measured as annualised revenue divided by the power required. It added more than $25 billion of new customer commitments early in the quarter, and its contracted power rose from about 3.7 gigawatts at 30 June to about 4.2 gigawatts at 11 August. It named no customers.
- Microsoft (reported 10 September). Bloomberg reported that Microsoft plans to take its capacity from about 12 gigawatts to more than 38 gigawatts by 2032, after shortages cost it business. Secondary accounts of that reporting say Temu signed with rival clouds and GitHub routed AI-agent traffic to AWS. Microsoft has not confirmed the figures.
- Broadcom (2 September). Chief executive Hock Tan listed the bottlenecks on the earnings call: "leading-edge silicon", "substrates", "HBM memory", and "land, power, and shell".

ByteNib found no change to hyperscaler list prices in September. The pressure is showing up in contract terms and availability first.

...

1. Budget for dearer, shorter capacity. Where you need GPU capacity next year, price it at today's market, not last year's contracts, and compare the premium for short terms with the risk of a long one.
2. Put suppliers' balance sheets in due diligence. For every AI capacity supplier, check free cash flow, customer concentration and who is financing the build. Oracle's negative cash flow, Nscale's two main customers and the new vendor-financing structures are all public.
3. Design for the outage you will actually get. Google's us-central1 outage on 1 September lasted four hours and eleven minutes. Technicians unplugged every fibre path during routine maintenance, taking out two zones at once. Critical AI and data workloads need to survive losing a region, not just a zone.
4. Expect the grid cost in your own projects. Anyone building or leasing new US data-centre capacity should expect demands to pay for grid upgrades and post real financial security, with Texas the partial exception for now.
5. Do not add backlogs together. When a vendor, analyst or board paper cites trillion-dollar AI commitments, ask how much is new this quarter and how much is counted twice.

results.title: Vera Rubin is 10× more efficient. You still can’t rent it cheap.
highlights:
The first Vera Rubin cloud instances are live — CoreWeave, Google Cloud’s A5X, Azure, OCI and Nebius are ramping them now, with production spinning up across NVIDIA’s partners. The number everyone is quoting is “10× lower cost per token than Blackwell.” It’s a real result and a big deal for the industry — but if you’re deciding whether to rent or buy for your own inference, it does not mean what it sounds like, and it will not show up on your bill this quarter.

The newest GPU is never the cheapest to rent. The per-hour ladder rises with each generation; Rubin lands premium and price-unknown. The efficiency win reaches you indirectly.

...

NVIDIA’s claim is precisely “~10× more tokens per megawatt” and “one-tenth the cost per million tokens” versus a GB200 NVL72 rack; CoreWeave independently reports ~10× the tokens/second per megawatt. Notice the unit: this is an energy-efficiency figure at the rack level, not a rental price. It becomes a 10× cost reduction only when power is your dominant cost and the rack is fully utilized — the vendor’s best case. No cloud has published a Rubin $/hour or $/token rate, and there’s a reason: first-wave supply is scarce and hyperscaler-reserved, with TSMC’s CoWoS packaging sold out until roughly Q4 2026. A launch-generation part is always priced at a premium while it’s rationed.

...

Look at the ladder. Today’s neocloud medians run about $2.00/hr for an A100, $4.17 for an H100, $4.50 for an H200, $7.88 for a B200, and ~$12 for a still-scarce B300. Each newer generation launched more expensive per hour, not less — because you’re paying for scarcity and peak demand, and the efficiency gains are amortized by the operator over time. Rubin will slot in at the top of that ladder, not the bottom. “Newest = cheapest per token” is true in a datacenter’s power budget; it is false on a rental invoice for months after launch.

...

Indirectly, and with a lag. First, through API prices: as providers stand up Rubin capacity to serve open models (DeepSeek, GLM, Qwen), the cost floor for tokens drops, and competition pushes per-token API rates down over the following quarters — the same dynamic that collapsed open-weight serving prices in August. Second, through the second-hand and rental markets for the last generation: as demand rotates to Rubin, Hopper and Blackwell rentals stay flat-to-down (H100 has been flat ~$4/hr for 90 days) and a wave of used H100/H200 will eventually hit the market, exactly as A100s did. That’s the channel a local builder should actually watch.

...

Rent / API — strongest case of the year. Don’t chase a first-wave Rubin instance; rent Hopper or Blackwell (cheap and flat) for your own jobs, and let the 10× reach you as falling API prices. Keep commitments short so you can ride the markdowns. Buy a datacenter GPU — worst timing of the year. This is my July–August point made concrete: owning is a bet against progress, and the progress just shipped. Purchasing an H100/H200/Blackwell today means buying at the moment a 10×-efficiency generation comes online and CoWoS relief threatens to loosen supply — your residual value is the casualty. Buy only for privacy, offline, or genuinely steady high utilization. Local desk: Rubin is an NVL72 datacenter rack; none of it plugs into your tower. Its gift to you is cheaper inference APIs now and, in 2027, cheap used Hopper/Blackwell bandwidth cards — that second-hand wave, not this launch, is your buy signal.

results.title: Running AI Workloads in the Cloud: GPU Cost and Scaling in 2026 | Vikgol
highlights:
The same NVIDIA H100 rents for around $1.38 per GPU-hour on a marketplace and $12.29 on Azure. Identical silicon, identical memory, a twelvefold spread — the only variable is who is selling it. And that spread is still not the most expensive decision most teams get wrong.

...

In July 2026, an NVIDIA H100 80GB rented for as little as $1.38 per GPU-hour on marketplace and boutique clouds, and as much as $12.29 on Azure's on-demand instances. Google Cloud listed its eight-GPU H100 node at $88.49 an hour, roughly $11.06 per GPU.

Same chip. Same memory. Twelvefold spread.

...

Pricing model — per-token API, serverless, on-demand, spot, or reserved. Hourly rate — which provider and which GPU.

...

## The Price Spread Is Real, and Exploitable

| Where you rent it | H100 per GPU-hour | What you give up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spot / interruptible | $1.25 – $1.49 | Reclaimed with 30 seconds to 2 minutes notice |
| Marketplace (Vast.ai, similar) | $1.38 – $2.00 | Host variability, no SLA, uneven reliability |
| Neo-clouds (Lambda, Runpod, Spheron) | $2.00 – $3.00 | Smaller regional footprint, fewer managed services |
| Market average, early 2026 | ~$3.11 | — |
| AWS P5 on-demand | ~$12.29 | Nothing — you are paying for ecosystem and SLA |
| Azure ND H100 v5 | $11 – $13 | Nothing — same |

...

Data egress on hyperscalers runs $0.08–$0.12 per GB. Moving a 2TB training dataset out of AWS costs over $160 before you have done any compute. For multi-cloud setups — training on one provider, serving on another — egress can quietly exceed the GPU bill. Model it before you architect around it.

...

An H100 at $3.99 an hour, running continuously, costs roughly $35,000 per GPU-year — more than buying the card outright. An eight-GPU node runs $49 an hour at CoreWeave or $55 at AWS: $36,000 to $40,000 a month at full utilisation.

Now apply the number nobody wants to measure. Most teams running dedicated GPU instances are somewhere between 15% and 40% utilised. At 25% utilisation, you are paying four times the effective rate — which means a $1.38 GPU sitting idle three-quarters of the time costs more per unit of work than a $3.00 GPU running flat out.

...

The crossover arrives inside a year for genuinely sustained workloads. An H100 at $3.99/hour is about $35,000 per GPU-year at full utilisation, against roughly $25,000–$40,000 to buy the card — before the server, networking, power, cooling and someone to operate it.

...

Utilisation is uncertain

Which is most of the time, especially in the first year of a product. Renting buys optionality, and optionality is worth a premium when your load forecast is really a guess.

results.title: What an H100 Is Worth Today, and What It Teaches B300 and Vera Rubin Lenders | GPU Appraisals
highlights:
The H100 is the first AI GPU to run through a full lending cycle. Since it launched in October 2022, lenders have financed H100 nodes at shortage prices, watched rental rates halve, and seen Blackwell reprice the fleet. Loans written in 2023 are now three years into their terms. What that collateral is worth today is the best evidence we have for how to underwrite B300 now and Vera Rubin next.

...

On paper, it was the most stable asset price in data center history.

The secondary market told a different story, and it moved in both directions. In April 2022, before shipping began, a Japanese retailer took H100 preorders at about $33,000 to $36,500 per card (TweakTown, PC Gamer). A year later, eBay listings for H100 cards ran from about $40,000 to just under $46,000 (CNBC). By mid-2023, complete 8-GPU HGX H100 SXM servers were quoted at $300K to $380K depending on specs and support (GPU Utils). Silicon Data, which analyzed thousands of listings from June 2024 through December 2025, found used and refurbished H100s listed as high as $50,000 per GPU in mid-2024. That is roughly $400K a node, above the new-unit sticker. Asking prices then fell hard as supply returned and buyers regained leverage.

So the sticker was wrong both ways. In the shortage it understated what a node would fetch. A year later it overstated it. A lender who sized an advance

...

Look at the right edge of the chart. Hashrate Index's AI Hardware Price Index put the median asking price for a new 8-GPU HGX H100 node at $324K on August 31, 2026, and for a refurbished node at $246K. Both are asks, not trades. Our anonymized example appraisal put fair market value at $214K a node on an income approach. The executed secondary sale of that same equipment came in at $121K.

...

Rental assumptions fared worse: a model built on early-2024 rates of more than $7 per GPU-hour now faces rates under $3.

...

Collateral value is what a buyer pays. A buyer pays for earning power, and a GPU's earning power is its rental rate.

That side of the market has been just as unstable. AIMultiple's rental index shows the median posted H100 rate falling from more than $7 in early 2024 to under $3 in 2026. Silicon Data's H100 Neo-Cloud index read $2.75 on July 27, 2026, up 7% since early May, and SemiAnalysis data shows one-year H100 contract rates rising from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026. Both things are true: the rate has more than halved from the shortage peak, and it is rising again because demand keeps outrunning supply. On NVIDIA's August 26 earnings call, CFO Colette Kress guided fiscal 2028 revenue growth of about 70%, said customer forecasts point to demand roughly doubling, and called the outlook supply constrained.

Meanwhile the generation above is re-rating. Silicon Data's neo-cloud indices show the H200, with 141 GB of HBM3e against the H100's 80 GB, rising 14.4% in rental rate from May to late July 2026, twice the H100's 7.0%. Over those twelve weeks the H200 premium ran from 5% down to 0.4%, then up to a 16.2% peak. B200 spot sits higher still. When the newer chip earns 10% to 15% more per hour, the older chip's residual value is being repriced whether or not anyone updates the spreadsheet.

...

The B300 is where the H100 was in 2023: newly shipping, supply-constrained and expensive. Hashrate Index put the median asking price for an air-cooled 8-GPU HGX B300 node at $544K on August 31, 2026, 1.68 times the new H100 ask.
